a: a friend in name and nothing more
t: Ben Sira comes back to friendship
p: The book's long teaching on friends (6:5-17) returns here, now with a warning about the friend who turns.
b: Friendship is one of Ben Sira's favorite subjects. Chapter 6 told the reader to test a friend before trusting him (6:7) and called a faithful friend "a sturdy shelter" (6:14). Chapters 22 and 27 warned that a betrayed secret ends a friendship. Here the teacher starts again from the bitter end: the friend who was only a friend "in name." The Hebrew of manuscripts B and D says the same thing in fewer words: "there is a friend who is a friend by name." Proverbs knows both kinds too (Proverbs 18:24). Ben Sira's advice is practical, not cynical: friends are tested by trouble (37:4), so the reader should look for the godly friend of 37:12.

a: a grief that comes close to death
p: The Greek phrase "grief to death" is the one Jesus uses of himself in Gethsemane.
b: The Greek says the grief is heōs thanatou, "as far as death." A grief so heavy it could kill is an old Hebrew way of speaking: Jonah is angry "even to death" (Jonah 4:9). In Gethsemane Jesus says, "My soul is crushed with grief, enough to kill me" (Mark 14:34), using the same two words in Greek, heōs thanatou. No one needs to suppose Mark is quoting Sirach. Both draw on the same idiom. But a reader of the Gospels may notice that what Ben Sira names as the worst grief, a friend turned enemy, is also what Jesus faced that night (Mark 14:18).
orig: λύπη ἔνι ἕως θανάτου (lypē eni heōs thanatou)

a: O evil scheming
p: The Greek has "wicked thought." The Hebrew has the word that later Jews used for the evil inclination.
b: The Greek enthymēma means a thought or a plan. The Hebrew of manuscripts B and D reads differently: "Alas, the evil one says, 'Why was I formed (notsarti) like this?'" The verb comes from the same root as yetser, "what is formed, inclination" (Genesis 6:5; Genesis 8:21). Ben Sira has already used yetser for the human power of choice (15:14). Later rabbis spoke of the yetser hara', the evil inclination. The Hebrew line here may be an early step toward that idea: evil itself complains that it was made to fill the world with deceit. The grandson's Greek turns the cry into a plain address to wicked scheming.
orig: ὦ πονηρὸν ἐνθύμημα (ō ponēron enthymēma); Hebrew הוי רע יאמר מדוע כן נוצרתי

a: for the sake of his stomach
t: A friend for his stomach, or a friend in battle?
p: The Greek companion helps for food; the Hebrew friend fights the stranger at your side.
b: The Greek line can be read two ways. Either the companion works with his friend only to be fed, and so is the fair-weather friend of 37:4, or he is a real help who, when war comes, takes up the shield. The Hebrew of manuscript D is clearer and kinder: "A good friend fights against a stranger and holds up the shield against enemies." The Greek translator seems to have read or heard a different word than "fights," and so produced "for the sake of his stomach." The Plain keeps the Greek, which is the text the churches received, and leaves the line as double-edged as it is.
orig: χάριν γαστρός (charin gastros), 'for the belly's sake'

a: slip from your soul
p: Ben Sira's Greek uses psychē, "soul," for the inner self: mind, desire and life together.
b: The Greek psychē stands for the Hebrew nefesh, the living self. It is the seat of desire (37:27-28), memory (here) and character (37:12, "whose soul is like your own soul"). It does not yet mean a part of a person that lives on after death, as it does in the Wisdom of Solomon (Wisdom of Solomon 3:1). Ben Sira expects no life after death for the individual (41:4). The Plain keeps "soul" where the Greek has it, so that readers can follow the word through the book, and uses "heart" only for kardia.
orig: ψυχή (psychē); Hebrew נפש (nefesh)

a: Perhaps he is casting lots over you
p: The Greek pictures an adviser who gambles with your fate. The Hebrew asks why it should fall to him.
b: Lots were thrown to decide things, from dividing the land to choosing a man for a task (Proverbs 16:33). An adviser who "casts the lot" over you treats your affairs as his game. The Hebrew of manuscripts B and D ends the verse with a question: "why should it fall to him?" The verb "fall" (nafal) is the word used for a lot that falls (Jonah 1:7). The grandson seems to have turned the Hebrew wording into the picture of a lot being thrown. Either way the warning is the same: find out what an adviser stands to gain before you take his advice.
orig: μή ποτε βάλῃ ἐπὶ σοὶ κλῆρον (mē pote balē epi soi klēron)

a: a woman what to do about her rival
p: The "rival" is another wife of the same husband, as Peninnah was to Hannah.
b: Where a man had more than one wife, each was the other's "rival" (Hebrew tsarah). Peninnah was Hannah's (1 Samuel 1:6), and the law forbade marrying a woman's sister "as a rival" to her (Leviticus 18:18). The Hebrew of manuscripts B and D has tsarah here, and the Greek gives its meaning, "her rival wife." The whole list that follows works the same way: never ask advice from someone whose interest runs against the advice. The merchant wants the trade, the buyer wants a low price, the coward wants to avoid the war.

a: a godly man
p: The Greek eusebēs, "godly, devout," is the word the Plain renders "godly" throughout this part.
b: Eusebēs describes a person whose life is turned toward God. In this part it stands at 37:12, 39:27 and 43:33, always "godly"; its opposite asebēs is "ungodly" (39:30; 41:5-10). The godly adviser is defined at once: he "keeps the commandments" and shares your outlook. For Ben Sira, piety is not a feeling but keeping the law (19:20). The Hebrew of manuscripts B and D has "one who is always in fear," that is, a man who fears God, "whom you know keeps the commandment."
orig: εὐσεβής (eusebēs)

a: seven watchmen posted on a high lookout
p: Your own inner sense can see further than seven guards on a tower.
b: Seven is the number of fullness. A city with seven lookouts on its walls would be well guarded. Ben Sira says a person's own soul can warn him better than that. Proverbs has a similar picture: "The human breath is the LORD's lamp, / searching through every inner room of the belly" (Proverbs 20:27). Ben Sira's point is practical. After weighing other people's advice, trust what your heart tells you (37:13), and then pray (37:15).

a: ask the Most High
p: Ben Sira's favorite name for God in the Greek is Hypsistos, "the Most High."
b: The grandson often renders the Hebrew names of God with ho hypsistos, "the Most High." Here the Hebrew of manuscripts B and D simply has 'el, "God": "And with all these, pray to God." The Greek title echoes Genesis 14:18-22, where Melchizedek is priest of God Most High, and it was well known to Greek-speaking Jews of Egypt. The Plain keeps "the Most High" for hypsistos and "the Lord" for kyrios. Because the Greek never writes the divine name, the Plain never uses "the LORD" in capitals in this book.
orig: Ὕψιστος (Hypsistos); Hebrew אל ('el)

a: The heart leaves a track when it changes
t: The heart and its four branches
p: The Greek is short and hard. The Hebrew says the heart is the root that sends up four branches.
b: Swete's text, from Codex Vaticanus, reads literally "a track of change for the heart." Other copies have "of the heart." Either way, the heart's changes show on the outside. The Hebrew of manuscripts B and D is a plant picture: "The root of plans is the heart; / four branches it puts out" (D has the word sharvitim, "shoots"). The four are good and evil, life and death (37:18). The Plain keeps the Greek's "track" and joins the two verses with a colon, as the sense requires.
orig: ἴχνος ἀλλοιώσεως καρδίᾳ (ichnos alloiōseōs kardia); Hebrew עקר תחבולות לבב

a: good and evil, life and death
t: Life and death, and the tongue
p: Moses set life and death before Israel. Ben Sira says the tongue decides between them.
b: The pairs come from Deuteronomy: "See, today I am placing before you life and what is good, death and what is bad" (Deuteronomy 30:15). Ben Sira has used them before: "Before people are life and death" (15:17). Here he adds a surprising master over all four: the tongue. Proverbs says the same: "Death and life are in the tongue's hand" (Proverbs 18:21). James later calls the tongue "a small member" that "brags of big things" (James 3:5). The Hebrew of manuscript B ends "and the one who rules them completely is the tongue."

a: One man is clever and teaches many
p: Verses 19-26 sort the wise into four kinds by whom their wisdom serves.
b: The section compares four wise men. The first teaches others but cannot help himself (37:19). The second talks cleverly and is hated (37:20-21). The third is wise for himself, and his words can be trusted (37:22). The fourth is wise for his people, and his name lives on (37:23-26). The Hebrew of manuscript D, and the margin of manuscript B, is sharper still: "There is a wise man who is wise for many, / but for himself he is a fool." The point is that wisdom is judged by its fruit, and the best wisdom serves the community, the work Ben Sira gives the scribe in 39:1-11.

a: the days of Israel cannot be counted
t: One life is short; Israel lives on
p: Ben Sira has no hope of personal life after death, but Israel's life has no end.
b: A man's days are numbered, but the people's are not. For Ben Sira this is the comfort that takes the place of personal survival: a person lives on in Israel and in a good name (37:26; 41:11-13; 44:13-15). The Hebrew of manuscript D calls Israel "Jeshurun," the poetic name of Deuteronomy 32:15 and Deuteronomy 33:5, and manuscript B has "Jeshurun" in its margin. The hope of Daniel 12:2, that the dead will wake, goes beyond it.

a: My child
p: The Greek teknon means "child"; the Hebrew behind it has bni, "my son," the address of a teacher to a pupil.
b: Ben Sira speaks as a father to a son, the way Proverbs does (Proverbs 1:8). The Hebrew of manuscripts B and D has beni, "my son," at 37:27, and again at 38:9 and 38:16. The grandson's Greek has teknon, "child." The Plain follows the Greek with "My child." The first hearers were young men in training (51:23), and "son" was the teacher's word for a pupil, as it still is in some Jewish schools.
orig: τέκνον (teknon); Hebrew בני (beni)

a: ends in a sick stomach
p: The Greek word is cholera, a doctors' term for violent vomiting and loose bowels, not the modern disease.
b: Greek doctors named cholera after cholē, "bile." It meant a sudden sickness of vomiting and diarrhea, the kind that follows a feast. English took the word for a different disease much later. The Hebrew of manuscript B says that the one who eats too much "comes to zara'," the rare word for the loathing that the Israelites felt when they had eaten quail for a month, "until it comes out of your nostrils and turns your stomach" (Numbers 11:20). Ben Sira's advice on eating (34:12-31 and here) sounds like a doctor's, and it leads straight into his praise of doctors.
orig: χολέρα (cholera); Hebrew זרא (zara')

a: with the honors due him
p: Greek timē means both "honor" and "price." The honor due a doctor may include paying him.
b: The verse says literally, "Honor a doctor, for your needs, with his honors." The Greek timē can mean the respect owed to someone and also a price or fee, so "his honors" may include his payment, as "honor" for elders does in 1 Timothy 5:17-18. The Hebrew of manuscript B begins differently: "Make a friend of the doctor before you need him." Its margin and manuscript D have a variant form of the same line. The Latin ("Honor the physician because of need") follows the Greek. Either way, the advice is to treat the doctor well, and not only once you are sick.
orig: τιμαῖς αὐτοῦ (timais autou); Hebrew רעי רופא לפני צרכו

a: for it was the Lord who created him
t: Compared with the Bible: doctors and faith
p: Ben Sira gives the doctor a place in God's plan. The Hebrew Bible is mostly silent, once critical, never forbidding.
b: Goes beyond. No book of the Hebrew Bible praises doctors. It names God as Israel's healer (Exodus 15:26). It once blames King Asa because "he did not seek the LORD, only the healers" (2 Chronicles 16:12). Yet it shows remedies used with God's approval, such as Isaiah's figs for Hezekiah (Isaiah 38:21). Agrees with the New Testament. Jesus says that "sick people do" need a doctor (Matthew 9:12). Paul calls Luke "the beloved doctor" (Colossians 4:14). Ben Sira puts the two together: God heals (38:9), and God made the doctor and his medicines (38:1, 4, 12). Readers who do not count Sirach as Scripture find the same balance in James 5:14 and 1 Timothy 5:23.
r: Exodus 15:26; 2 Chronicles 16:12; Isaiah 38:21; Matthew 9:12; Colossians 4:14; James 5:14; 1 Timothy 5:23

a: he will receive a gift from the king
p: Kings kept doctors and paid them well. Ben Sira's readers knew the court physician as a man of standing.
b: The Hebrew of manuscript B says the same: "from the king he will receive gifts." In Egypt Joseph orders "the physicians" in his service to embalm Jacob (Genesis 50:2). In the Hellenistic kingdoms of Ben Sira's day, the Ptolemies in Egypt and the Seleucids in Syria, doctors served the royal households and were rewarded. That is why the doctor "holds his head high" and is admired by "the great" (38:3). Ben Sira himself moved among rulers (39:4), and he speaks of the doctor as one professional man of another.

a: Out of the earth the Lord created remedies
p: Genesis Rabbah quotes Ben Sira by name: God brings up medicines from the earth.
b: The rabbis did not count Ben Sira as Scripture, but they quoted him. Genesis Rabbah 10:6 cites "Bar Sira": "God produced drugs from the earth with which the physician heals the wound, and with which the pharmacist mixes his compounds" (Sefaria's translation). That is a close form of 38:4 and 38:7-8. The Hebrew of manuscript B reads, "God brings out remedies from the earth, / and let a man of understanding not reject them." The midrash goes on to say that every blade of grass has a heavenly power over it. Ben Sira's thought is simpler: medicine is part of God's good creation (39:16).
orig: Κύριος ἔκτισεν ἐκ γῆς φάρμακα (Kyrios ektisen ek gēs pharmaka); Hebrew אל מארץ מוציא תרופות

a: Did not a piece of wood once turn water sweet
p: Ben Sira reads the miracle of Exodus 15 as God showing the healing power he put into a plant.
b: At Marah the water was bitter. Moses "cried out to the LORD, and the LORD pointed out to him a piece of wood. He threw it into the water, and the water turned sweet" (Exodus 15:25). Right after, God says, "I am the LORD, your healer" (Exodus 15:26). Ben Sira takes the story as proof that God has put healing power into created things. Whose power does the verse mean? The Greek autou can be "its" (the wood's) or "his" (God's). The Hebrew of manuscript B has "his strength," with "their strength" in its margin. The Plain chooses "its," since the subject is remedies, but God's power is made known through them either way (38:6).
orig: τὴν ἰσχὺν αὐτοῦ (tēn ischyn autou), 'its/his strength'

a: the ointment-maker
p: The Greek myrepsos was a maker of perfumes and salves, the pharmacist of the ancient world.
b: The myrepsos mixed oils, spices and resins into perfumes, ointments and medicines. The Septuagint uses the same craft for the holy anointing oil, "a blend mixed by the perfumer's art" (Exodus 30:25). The Hebrew of manuscript B has roqeach, the spice-mixer. The doctor diagnosed and treated; the ointment-maker prepared the remedies. Ben Sira honors both as God's instruments.
orig: μυρεψός (myrepsos); Hebrew רוקח (roqeach)

a: So his works never come to an end
p: God's works, which go on through medicine, or the pharmacist's? The Hebrew points to God.
b: The Greek "his works" could mean the pharmacist's work, which is never finished, or God's work of creation, which goes on through the remedies he made. The Hebrew of manuscript B reads, "so that his work may not cease, / and sound wisdom from humankind." That reads most naturally of God. On this reading, every cure is God continuing what he began. The second line, "peace over the face of the earth," uses the Greek eirēnē, which often renders shalom, health and wholeness.
orig: οὐ μὴ συντελέσῃ ἔργα αὐτοῦ (ou mē syntelesē erga autou)

a: he is the one who will heal you
p: Ben Sira's order: pray, turn from sin, give an offering, and then call the doctor.
b: The sick person turns first to God, who "heals every sickness you have" (Psalm 103:3; Exodus 15:26). The Hebrew of manuscript B has "pray to God, for he will heal." Then come repentance (38:10) and an offering (38:11), and only after that, the doctor (38:12). Ben Sira does not set prayer against medicine. He puts both in order under God. The New Testament pattern is similar: "Is one of you ill? Let him send for the elders of the church. Let them pray over him" (James 5:14). Jewish teaching on whether to call a doctor is set out on the medicine page.

a: wash your heart clean of every sin
p: Ben Sira ties sickness to sin, as much of the Bible does. Job and John 9 warn against making it a rule.
b: Ben Sira tells the sick to put away wrongdoing before calling the doctor. Many biblical writers link sin and sickness (Psalm 38:3; Psalm 107:17; James 5:15). Others warn that the link is not automatic. Job's friends were wrong to accuse him (Job 42:7). Jesus says of the man born blind, "This man did not sin, and his parents did not sin" (John 9:3). Ben Sira's advice need not mean that every illness is a punishment. It can be read as a call to make peace with God while life is at risk.
r: Psalm 38:3; Psalm 107:17; James 5:15–16; Job 42:7; John 9:2–3; 1 Corinthians 11:30

a: a token portion of fine flour
p: Ben Sira tells the sick to bring the grain offering of Leviticus 2, using its own terms.
b: The Greek euōdia, "sweet smell," and mnēmosynon, "memorial portion," are the Septuagint's words for the "soothing smell" and the "token portion" of the grain offering: "He is to make this token portion go up in smoke on the altar" (Leviticus 2:2). The Hebrew of manuscript B has the Leviticus word 'azkarah, and Kahana's edition reads nichoach, "soothing smell," before it, where the leaf is now damaged. So the sick man goes to the Temple in Jerusalem before he goes to the doctor. Ben Sira, who loved the Temple service (50:1-21), takes it for granted.
orig: εὐωδίαν καὶ μνημόσυνον σεμιδάλεως (euōdian kai mnēmosynon semidaleōs); Hebrew ניחוח אזכרה

a: success lies in their hands
p: Verses 12-14 make doctors God's servants who pray for success in their work.
b: The doctor too is a man of prayer. He asks the Lord to bless his diagnosis and treatment (38:14). The Hebrew of manuscript B says, "for there is a time when success is in his hand, / for he too prays to God." This view, that God heals through means, became the usual Jewish and Christian position. The Talmud's ruling that "permission is granted to a doctor to heal" and the Catholic Catechism's call to take care of health are described on the medicine page. The minority who reject medicine for faith alone must argue against this passage, which Catholic and Orthodox Christians count as Scripture.

a: may he fall into a doctor's hands!
t: A curse, a joke, or a warning?
p: The Greek can be read as "let the sinner need a doctor." The Hebrew says the sinner acts proud before the doctor.
b: The Greek seems to say that sickness is the sinner's punishment: let him fall into the doctor's hands. Some readers take it as a wry joke at doctors, but that does not fit a passage that has just honored them. The Hebrew of manuscript B reads, "Whoever sins before his Maker / will act defiantly (yitgabber) before the doctor," that is, he will refuse treatment. Its margin has a second reading, "will be handed over into the hands of a doctor," which is close to the Greek. The Plain follows the Greek, with an exclamation mark to show that it is a wish.
orig: ἐμπέσοι εἰς χεῖρας ἰατροῦ (empesoi eis cheiras iatrou); Hebrew יתגבר לפני רופא

a: begin the lament
p: Weeping, beating the breast, a formal lament and a proper burial were duties owed to the dead.
b: The dead were washed and wrapped and buried the same day or the next. Mourners wept aloud and beat their breasts, and someone raised a lament, a set poem of grief (2 Samuel 1:17-27; Jeremiah 9:17-18). Neglecting a burial was a disgrace, and burying the dead was praised as a good work (Tobit 1:17). Ben Sira asks for real grief, done properly, "so that no one can speak against you" (38:17). Elsewhere he says that mourning for the dead lasts seven days (22:12).

a: for a day or two
p: A day or two of public weeping, then comfort. Ben Sira fears grief that destroys the living.
b: Ben Sira wants grief expressed but limited. "A day or two" seems short beside the seven days of 22:12, and readers have taken it two ways. Some think he means the most intense weeping, after which the formal mourning goes on. Others think he simply sets a firm limit, because "from grief comes death" (38:18). His concern is the living: "You will not help him, and you will hurt yourself" (38:21). Paul, who had a hope Ben Sira lacked, says Christians will not grieve "the way the others do, who have no hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

a: grief also should pass by
p: The Greek is obscure. Manuscript B of the Hebrew has no line for this verse.
b: The Greek reads literally, "In a leading-away, grief too passes by, / and the life of a poor man is against the heart." "Leading-away" may mean carrying the body to burial or being led away to calamity. The Plain takes the first: once the dead is carried out, grief should pass. Codex Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus have "remains" instead of "passes by," which reverses the sense, and the KJV follows them ("In affliction also sorrow remaineth"). Manuscript B goes straight from 38:18 to 38:20.
orig: ἐν ἀπαγωγῇ παραβαίνει καὶ λύπη (en apagōgē parabainei kai lypē)

a: there is no way back
t: Compared with the Bible: no return from death
p: Ben Sira agrees with the older books that the dead do not come back. He knows nothing yet of resurrection.
b: Agrees with much of the Hebrew Bible. David says of his dead child, "I am the one who will go to him. He will not come back to me" (2 Samuel 12:23), and Job says that "the one who goes down to Sheol never climbs back up" (Job 7:9). Falls short of the hope that Daniel 12:2 states and the New Testament proclaims. Ben Sira, writing about 180 BC, speaks of no resurrection. His comfort is a good name and the life of Israel (37:25-26; 41:11-13). For Catholic and Orthodox Christians, who count both Sirach and 2 Maccabees as Scripture, the fuller hope comes within their own Old Testament (2 Maccabees 7). The same silence about life after death appears in Ecclesiastes 9:10.
r: 2 Samuel 12:23; Job 7:9–10; Daniel 12:2; Ecclesiastes 9:10; 2 Maccabees 7:9; John 11:25

a: "Mine yesterday, and yours today."
p: The dead man speaks. In Latin the line became a famous gravestone saying.
b: Suddenly the dead man himself speaks: what happened to me yesterday will happen to you today. The Hebrew of manuscript B has "Remember his decree, for it is your decree: / to him yesterday, and to you today," without the dead man's own voice. The Latin Vulgate has the same words as the Greek: mihi heri, et tibi hodie, "to me yesterday, and to you today." Ben Sira gives the line not to frighten but to calm: since death is everyone's lot, the mourner should let the dead rest (38:23).
orig: ἐμοὶ ἐχθὲς καὶ σοὶ σήμερον (emoi echthes kai soi sēmeron)

a: A scribe's wisdom
p: A grammateus, "scribe," in Ben Sira's day was a scholar of the Scriptures and a public servant.
b: The Greek grammateus (Hebrew sofer) was first a man who could write: a secretary or a clerk. By Ben Sira's time the scribe was the learned man who studied and taught the law of Moses, as Ezra had been, "a scribe, an expert in Moses' law" (Ezra 7:6). The scribes of the Gospels belong to the same class (Matthew 23:2). Ben Sira was one of them, and 39:1-11 is in part a picture of himself.
orig: γραμματεύς (grammateus); Hebrew סופר (sofer)

a: the chance of leisure
p: The Greek scholē, "leisure," is the word that gave English "school."
b: The grandson chose the Greek word scholē. It meant free time, and then the use of free time for study and talk, and so a lecture or school. English "school" comes from it. Ben Sira's point is not that scholars are lazy, but that study needs time freed from manual work. The word comes back as a play on words: the scribe "busies himself" (ascholēthēsetai, literally "is kept from leisure") with prophecies (39:1), and "much hard work" (ascholia, "lack of leisure") was made for everyone (40:1).
orig: σχολή (scholē)

a: What wisdom can a plowman gain
t: An Egyptian satire of the trades
p: Ben Sira's tour of the trades has a famous Egyptian parallel, the Instruction of Kheti.
b: An Egyptian schoolbook of the Middle Kingdom, the Satire of the Trades (or Instruction of Kheti), has a father take his son to scribal school. He describes the misery of other jobs, smiths, potters, builders and farmers, and praises the scribe's career as "greater than any profession." It was copied in Egyptian scribal schools long after it was written. Scholars often compare it with 38:24-39:11. Verdict: the likeness of form is real and may well be known to Ben Sira, but the tone differs. The Egyptian mocks the workers. Ben Sira honors them: "each one is wise in his own work" (38:31), and the city cannot stand without them (38:32).

a: He gives his heart to cutting furrows
t: "He gives his heart" and "he lies awake"
p: A refrain runs through the trades, and then returns for the scribe in 39:5.
b: Each worker "gives his heart" to his task and "lies awake" over it (38:26, 27, 28, 30). The Greek words are kardian dōsei, "he will give his heart," and agrypnia, "sleeplessness." The Plain repeats the same English each time so the pattern can be heard. In 39:5 the scribe too "gives his heart," but to rising early to pray. Ezra had done the same: he "had given his heart to searching out the LORD's law" (Ezra 7:10). The worker's devotion is good, and the scholar's is the same devotion turned toward God.
orig: καρδίαν αὐτοῦ δώσει (kardian autou dōsei); ἀγρυπνία (agrypnia)

a: those who cut the engravings on seals
p: Engraving seals in hard stone was fine, slow work, done with drills and abrasives.
b: Seals were small carved stones, pressed into clay or wax to sign documents and close jars. The Bible knows the craft: "As a stonecutter engraves a seal, engrave the two stones with the names of Israel's sons" (Exodus 28:11), the stones on the high priest's shoulders. Ben Sira notes the cutter's patience as he varies the design to make each seal different.

a: hardens his skin
p: Vaticanus says the fire "hardens" the smith's flesh; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus say it "melts" it.
b: The two readings differ by one letter: pēxei, "will make firm, harden" (Vaticanus, followed by Swete), and tēxei, "will melt" (Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus). The KJV follows the second ("the vapour of the fire wasteth his flesh"). Both describe what a smith's life did to his body: skin dried and toughened by heat, or a body worn away by it. The Plain follows Vaticanus.
orig: πήξει (pēxei) / τήξει (tēxei)

a: spinning the wheel with his feet
p: By Ben Sira's time potters used a kick-wheel, turned with the feet while the hands shaped the clay.
b: Jeremiah watched a potter "at work on the wheel" (Jeremiah 18:3); the Hebrew there has two stones, a pair of wheels. Ben Sira describes the potter turning it "with his feet" and working the clay with his arm and feet (38:30). "Every pot he makes is counted" may mean he must make a set number to earn his living. The prophets used the potter as a picture of God shaping Israel (Jeremiah 18:6; Isaiah 64:8), and Ben Sira has used it himself (36:13). Here the potter is simply a hard-working man.

a: finishing the fine piece
t: The fine piece, or the glaze?
p: Vaticanus has charisma, "a thing of grace"; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus have chrisma, "the coating" or glaze.
b: Swete prints charisma, the reading of the first hand of Vaticanus: a gift, a lovely thing. A later corrector of Vaticanus, with Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus, has chrisma, an anointing or coating, which in a potter's shop would be the glaze. The KJV's "he applieth himself to lead it over" follows the coating reading. The Plain follows Swete with "the fine piece."
orig: χάρισμα (charisma) / χρῖσμα (chrisma)

a: they do not think through the covenant of judgment
t: Why workers did not sit as judges
p: Judging, teaching and writing proverbs needed long study, and the workers had no time for it.
b: The "covenant of judgment" seems to mean the laws and rulings by which a court decides. Judges, elders and teachers needed to know the law of Moses in depth. Workers who labored from dawn to dark could not gain that learning. Ben Sira is not saying they are worse people. They "keep the made world standing" (38:34). But public wisdom, in the assembly and the court, belongs to the scribe (39:4-10). Some readers find his view of class narrow. Christian readers recall that Jesus was called "the builder" (Mark 6:3) and that Paul made tents (Acts 18:3).

a: their prayer is in the work of their craft
p: A famous line: the craftsman's prayer is in his craft. It can mean their work is their prayer, or what they pray for.
b: The Greek says literally, "their prayer is in the working of a craft." It may mean that their prayers are about their work (that the pot will hold, the plow will cut). Or it may mean that the work itself is a kind of prayer, an offering of skill to God. The second sense fits the Bible's high view of skilled work (Exodus 31:3; Colossians 3:23). The Hebrew of this verse is not preserved in the Genizah manuscripts. Ben Sira's own next line moves on at once to the one who prays with words (39:1, 5).
orig: ἡ δέησις αὐτῶν ἐν ἐργασίᾳ τέχνης (hē deēsis autōn en ergasia technēs)

a: pondering the law of the Most High
t: Law, wisdom, prophecies: a three-part Scripture?
p: The scribe studies law, wisdom and prophecies, much as the prologue names three groups of books.
b: Ben Sira's scholar studies "the law of the Most High," "the wisdom of all the ancients" and "prophecies," then sayings, parables and proverbs (39:2-3). His grandson's prologue speaks of "the law and the prophets and the others who came after them." Some scholars see in both a Scripture already in three parts, like the later Jewish Torah, Prophets and Writings. Others think the lists are looser. "Wisdom of the ancients" may include wisdom from other nations, and the canon was not yet closed. Either way, the law comes first, as it does for Ben Sira everywhere (24:23).

a: busies himself with prophecies
p: A play on words: the man of leisure (38:24) is the one who is truly busy.
b: The verb ascholēthēsetai means "he will be occupied," literally "kept from leisure." It is built on scholē, the "leisure" a scribe needs (38:24). The grandson seems to enjoy the point: the scholar is freed from manual work only to be kept busy with the prophets.
orig: ἐν προφητείαις ἀσχοληθήσεται (en prophēteiais ascholēthēsetai)

a: the riddles of parables
p: The scribe's subjects are the very forms of Proverbs: sayings, figures and riddles.
b: Proverbs opens by promising its reader skill "for understanding a proverb and a figure, / what the wise say and the riddles they pose" (Proverbs 1:6). Ben Sira's scribe lives among the same forms. A parabolē in the Greek Bible renders Hebrew mashal, which covers proverbs, comparisons and stories with a hidden point. Jesus' parables belong to the same family, and Mark notes that they had to be explained (Mark 4:10-13, 34).
orig: ἐν αἰνίγμασι παραβολῶν (en ainigmasi parabolōn)

a: He passes through the lands of foreign nations
p: Ben Sira's ideal scribe serves rulers and travels abroad. He speaks of his own travels too (31:12).
b: Scribes served in courts and on embassies, and travel taught them how other peoples lived. Ben Sira says elsewhere, "I have seen much in my wanderings" (31:12). In his day Judea was ruled first by the Ptolemies of Egypt and then, from about 200 BC, by the Seleucids of Syria, so a Jerusalem scholar had reason to know foreign courts. Joseph and Daniel are the Bible's great examples of Israelites wise in foreign courts (Genesis 41:39-40; Daniel 1:19-20).

a: He gives his heart to rising at dawn
p: Ben Sira's ideal scholar begins with prayer, as the craftsman began with his task.
b: The same words used for the workers' devotion (38:26-30) now describe the scribe turning to God at dawn. He prays for himself and for forgiveness. Study, for Ben Sira, is worship, and wisdom is God's gift, not a human achievement: "If the Lord who is great so wills, a spirit of understanding will fill him" (39:6). Psalm 5:3 and Psalm 119:147 speak of morning prayer. Ezra is the Bible's model of such a scholar (Ezra 7:10).
r: 38:26–30; 39:6; Psalm 5:3; Psalm 119:147; Ezra 7:10; Wisdom of Solomon 7:7

a: a spirit of understanding will fill him
p: The scribe's insight comes from God, as Isaiah's ruler has "a spirit of wisdom and understanding."
b: The phrase echoes Isaiah's promised ruler, on whom the spirit of the LORD rests, "a spirit of wisdom and understanding" (Isaiah 11:2), and the Spirit that filled Bezalel with skill (Exodus 31:3). Ben Sira does not claim prophecy. He says only that wisdom is a gift God may choose to give. The Plain has a lowercase "spirit": the text speaks of a God-given gift of insight, though Christian readers will think of the Spirit who teaches (John 14:26).
orig: πνεύματι συνέσεως (pneumati syneseōs)

a: his name will live from generation to generation
t: Claude's theory: a self-portrait with a hope
p: This portrait of the scribe is likely Ben Sira's own hope for his name. His book has kept that name alive.
b: My suggestion: 39:1-11 is not only an ideal but Ben Sira's own program. He signs his book (50:27), invites students to his house of instruction (51:23), says he traveled (31:12) and has "set it down in writing" (39:32). The promise of a lasting name (39:9-11) is the only afterlife he expects (41:11-13). That hope came true in a way he could not foresee: his name survives in Greek, Latin and Hebrew copies from Masada to the Cairo Genizah.

a: as full as the moon at mid-month
p: Ben Sira compares himself to the full moon: he is full of things to say.
b: The Greek dichomēnia is the middle of the month, when the moon is full. Israel's months began at the new moon, so the full moon fell near the fifteenth day, when Passover and the Feast of Booths begin (Leviticus 23:5-6, 34). Ben Sira uses the moon again in his hymn on creation (43:6-8) and for the high priest Simon (50:6).
orig: διχομηνία (dichomēnia)

a: you holy sons
p: Ben Sira addresses his pupils as hosioi, "holy" or "devout" ones.
b: The Greek hosios renders Hebrew chasid, "faithful, devout." The same Greek word at 39:24 is rendered "those who are holy." The pupils are called to blossom like a rose, give scent like incense and flower like the lily (39:13-14), the same garden images Wisdom uses of herself (24:13-17). The Hebrew of this passage is lost from manuscript B until 39:15.
orig: υἱοὶ ὅσιοι (huioi hosioi)

a: This is how you will speak your thanks
t: A hymn inside a book of teaching
p: Verses 16-35 are a hymn of praise, framed by the call to sing (39:14-15) and the closing blessing (39:35).
b: Ben Sira breaks off his teaching to give his pupils a song. It is built on refrains: "The Lord's works, every one of them, are good" (39:16, 33) and "No one may say..." (39:17, 21, 34). Manuscript B of the Hebrew preserves the hymn from 39:15. The Masada scroll keeps the ends of a few lines of 39:27-32, the earliest Hebrew text of the book. Hymns like this one would be sung with the lyre, the kinyra of 39:15, the Greek name for the Hebrew kinnor.

a: The Lord's works, every one of them, are very good
p: The refrain takes its words from the end of the creation story.
b: At the end of the sixth day, "God looked at everything he had made, and there it was, very good" (Genesis 1:31). Ben Sira's hymn defends that verdict against complaint. If some things seem harmful, it is because they serve a purpose in God's time (39:16-17, 21, 34). Ecclesiastes says something close: "Everything he has made beautiful in its time" (Ecclesiastes 3:11). Paul writes that "Every created thing God made is good" (1 Timothy 4:4).

a: the water stood like a mound
p: The Red Sea crossing and the waters of creation stand behind this line.
b: At the sea, "the waters were heaped up. / Running streams stood up like a mound" (Exodus 15:8). The psalm of creation says, "He heaps up the sea's waters like a mound; / he lays the deeps away in storerooms" (Psalm 33:7). Ben Sira joins the two: by his word God controls the waters, at creation and at the Exodus. The Hebrew of manuscript B is damaged at the start of the verse but keeps "the word of his mouth, his storehouse."

a: as when he turned waters into salt
p: The Hebrew says God turned a watered land to salt, as with Sodom and the land of Psalm 107.
b: The Hebrew of manuscript B reads, "and he turned a watered land into salt." The psalm says God turns "orchard country into salt land, / because the people living there are evil" (Psalm 107:34). Readers have long thought of the Dead Sea region, once well watered (Genesis 13:10), after the fall of Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:24-26). Codex Alexandrinus and Ephraemi (C) move this line to the next verse.

a: Good things were made for good people from the start
t: Good things for the good, bad for sinners
p: The hymn's answer to the problem of evil: the same things bless the good and punish the wicked.
b: Ben Sira does not deny that harmful things exist: winds, hail, famine, wild beasts and the sword (39:28-30). He says they were created for a purpose, to punish sinners, and that even the good necessities of life (39:26) turn to harm for the wicked (39:27). This is the confident view of Proverbs and Deuteronomy. Job and Ecclesiastes press against it, since the righteous also suffer (Job 21:7; Ecclesiastes 7:15). Paul says something both like and unlike it: "all things work together toward good for those who love God" (Romans 8:28). Readers today differ on how far Ben Sira's answer holds. It is an answer of praise, not a complete theory.

a: The chief things a human life needs
p: Water, fire, iron, salt, flour, wheat, honey, milk, wine and oil, with clothing: a farmer's list of essentials.
b: The list is the life of a Judean household: water and fire for cooking, iron for tools, salt, flour and grain, honey, milk, "the blood of the grape" (wine, as in Genesis 49:11 and Deuteronomy 32:14), olive oil and clothing. Kahana's edition of manuscript B has "the best of wheat" (chelev chittah) beside milk (chalav), a play on two words spelled alike. Deuteronomy promises a land where "Its stones are iron" (Deuteronomy 8:9). Milk and honey recall the land "flowing with milk and honey."

a: Some winds were made to punish
p: The Greek pneumata, like the Hebrew ruchot, can be "winds" or "spirits."
b: Kahana's edition of manuscript B has ruchot, which, like the Greek pneumata, means winds or spirits. The context (fire, hail, famine) favors winds: God's storms used for judgment, as in Psalm 148:8 ("the storm wind that carries out his word"). Some readers, then and now, hear in it destroying spirits like the angel of 2 Samuel 24:16. Psalm 104:4 holds both together: "He makes the winds into his messengers." The Plain has "winds," as the Wisdom of Solomon's "the force of the winds" (Wisdom of Solomon 7:20).
orig: πνεύματα (pneumata); Hebrew רוחות (ruchot)
r: Psalm 148:8; Psalm 104:4; 2 Samuel 24:16; Wisdom of Solomon 7:20

a: They rejoice at his command
p: Even the destroying things obey with joy, like soldiers who wait for orders.
b: The punishing winds, beasts and weapons are pictured as servants who are glad to be sent and never overstep their orders. Job 37:12 says the clouds go "to do whatever he commands them," and Psalm 148:8 has fire, hail and wind carrying out his word. The point is comfort: nothing in creation is out of God's control. The Masada scroll keeps a few letters of this verse.

a: set it down in writing
p: Ben Sira is the first Israelite teacher whose book we know by his own name.
b: The teacher says he became sure of this long ago and has written it down. Earlier wisdom books are anonymous or put under a famous name such as Solomon. Ben Sira signs his own book (50:27). His grandson, translating it in Egypt after 132 BC, says in the prologue that his grandfather wrote so that lovers of learning could live by the law.

a: Much hard work was made for every person
p: The curse of Genesis 3 and the weariness of Ecclesiastes lie behind this verse.
b: "By the sweat of your face you will eat bread" (Genesis 3:19) is the heavy yoke laid on "the sons of Adam." The Hebrew of manuscript B opens with 'eseq gadol, "a great task," the kind of word Ecclesiastes uses: "It is an evil task, which God has given human beings to busy themselves with" (Ecclesiastes 1:13). In the grandson's Greek the word is ascholia, "lack of leisure," the third use of the scribe's word-family (38:24; 39:1). No one escapes the yoke, from king to beggar (40:3-4).
orig: ἀσχολία μεγάλη (ascholia megalē); Hebrew עסק גדול

a: the mother of all
p: The earth is the mother everyone returns to. The Hebrew uses the very words Genesis uses for Eve.
b: The Hebrew of manuscript B reads, "until the day he returns to the mother of all living" ('em kol chai). Those are the words that name Eve: "she was the mother of everyone living" (Genesis 3:20). Here they name the earth, the mother from whom humans were taken (Genesis 2:7) and to whom they go back (Genesis 3:19). Job says, "Naked I came out from my mother's womb, / and naked I will return there" (Job 1:21), with the same double meaning of womb and earth.
r: Genesis 3:20; Genesis 2:7; Genesis 3:19; Job 1:21; Ecclesiastes 5:15; Psalm 139:15

a: for the wearer of violet and a crown
p: Violet (hyacinth blue) was the dye of kings and priests. Unbleached flax was the poor man's cloth.
b: The Greek hyakinthos is a blue-violet dye made from sea snails, used for the tabernacle curtains and the high priest's robe (Exodus 28:31) and worn by kings. Its opposite is ōmolinon, "raw linen," flax cloth not yet bleached or finished. The Hebrew of manuscript B has "from the one who wears a turban and a diadem (tsits) / to the one who wears a garment of skin" (the last word as Kahana read it; the leaf is now damaged). The turban and diadem were the high priest's (Exodus 28:36-37). From the top of society to the bottom, the same fears come (40:5).
orig: ὑάκινθον (hyakinthon); ὠμόλινον (ōmolinon)

a: it is as if he were on watch by day
p: Ben Sira describes the nightmare of a man who dreams he is fleeing a battle.
b: Even in sleep there is no rest. The sleeper is on guard, sees terrors and wakes, relieved, at the moment of escape (40:7). Ben Sira has already warned that dreams deceive (31:1-8). Job, too, complains that God frightens him "with dreams" at night (Job 7:13-14). Kahana's edition of manuscript B ends the verse "like a survivor fleeing from a pursuer."

a: seven times more to sinners
p: Seven times means in full measure. Sinners suffer the same troubles, and more.
b: "Sevenfold" is a biblical way to say "in full": Cain would be avenged sevenfold (Genesis 4:15), and Leviticus threatens punishment "seven times" for sins (Leviticus 26:18). Ben Sira's claim that the wicked suffer more than others is the confident teaching of 39:25-30, and it leads to his strongest example, the flood (40:10).

a: the flood came because of them
p: The flood is the great example of judgment on the lawless.
b: In Genesis God saw that "the earth is full of violence" (Genesis 6:13) and sent the flood. Ben Sira will come back to it in the Praise of the Fathers, where Noah is "a remnant for the earth" (44:17). Jesus uses the flood as a warning (Matthew 24:37-39), and 2 Peter as a pattern of judgment (2 Peter 2:5).

a: die away like a loud thunderclap in the rain
p: Ill-gotten wealth is a wadi in flood: loud for a moment, then dry.
b: A wadi in Judea can roar with water after a storm and be dry the next day. The Hebrew of manuscript B says "from strength to strength (or sand to sand), like a mighty stream, / like a great channel in a thunderclap of voices." The unjust man's riches make a noise and vanish. Job's friends are "like a creek that fails" (Job 6:15). Ben Sira's next lines set beside this the things that last: faithfulness, kindness, almsgiving (40:12, 17).

a: While he opens his hands, he is glad
p: The line can mean a generous man rejoices, or that a greedy man is glad while he grabs.
b: The Greek simply says, "In his opening his hands he will rejoice." Opening the hands is the gesture of giving (Deuteronomy 15:8, 11), so it may contrast a generous man with the lawbreakers of the next line. But the setting is the unjust man of 40:13, so it may mean that he is glad while he takes, and then vanishes. The Hebrew of manuscript B and the Masada scroll read "when he lifts up his palms," and B continues "they rejoice." The Plain keeps the Greek's double sense.
orig: ἐν τῷ ἀνοῖξαι αὐτὸν χεῖρας εὐφρανθήσεται

a: their roots are unclean, on a cliff of bare rock
p: The ungodly family is a plant with no soil, like the seed on rock in Jesus' parable.
b: A root on a sheer rock cannot go deep, and the first flood tears it out (40:16). Psalm 1 sets the righteous man "like a tree planted by streams of water" against the wicked who are like chaff. Jesus' parable has seed that fell "on the rock" and withered for lack of moisture (Luke 8:6). Ben Sira applies the picture to families: the ungodly will not spread branches into later generations (41:5-7).
r: Psalm 1:3–4; Job 8:11–19; Luke 8:6; 41:5–7; Wisdom of Solomon 4:3–5

a: almsgiving remains forever
p: The Greek eleēmosynē, giving to the poor, here stands for Hebrew tsedaqah, "righteousness."
b: Ben Sira's Greek uses eleēmosynē, "mercy, alms," for what the Hebrew of manuscript B calls tsedaqah, "righteousness": "and righteousness will be established forever." By his day tsedaqah often meant charity to the poor, as it still does in Jewish use. The same pairing is in 40:24. Tobit says "alms rescue from death" (Tobit 12:9), and Proverbs says "righteousness rescues from death" (Proverbs 10:2). Whether giving to the poor takes away sin is asked on the Tobit 4 card.
orig: ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosynē); Hebrew צדקה (tsedaqah)

a: but better than both
t: "Better than both": a ladder of sayings
p: Ten sayings in a row name two good things and then a third that is better.
b: Verses 18-27 form a chain. Each names two good things, then says something is "better than both." The chain climbs to its peak in the fear of the Lord (40:26-27). The Hebrew of manuscript B uses the same refrain, umishnehem, "and above the two of them," and has one more pair at 40:19 than the Greek. Proverbs has "better than" sayings (Proverbs 15:16-17; 16:8), but Ben Sira's chain is his own.

a: but better than both is a blameless wife
t: Ben Sira's praise of a good wife
p: Three times in this chain (40:19, 23, 25) a wife is the better thing.
b: A blameless wife (40:19), a wife with her husband (40:23) and a wife who is valued (40:25, but see the variant) are counted above children, friends and gold. The Hebrew of manuscript B has at 40:19 "a wife who is desired" and at 40:23 "a sensible wife," which recalls "a wife with good sense comes from the LORD" (Proverbs 19:14). Ben Sira's sayings about women are mixed (25:13-26; 26:1-4; 42:9-14). Readers who find him harsh elsewhere point to verses like these. Readers who defend him say he honors women in their roles as he saw them.

a: Pipe and harp sweeten a tune
p: The aulos was a reed pipe; the psaltērion a stringed instrument plucked with the fingers.
b: The aulos was a double reed pipe, played at feasts and funerals (Matthew 9:23). The psaltērion renders the Hebrew nevel, a harp or large lyre. The Hebrew of manuscript B has chalil and nevel, the pipe and harp of Isaiah 5:12. Better than music, says Ben Sira, is "a pleasant tongue," or as the Hebrew has it, "a clear tongue."

a: almsgiving, which rescues
p: Tobit and Proverbs say the same: alms, or righteousness, rescues from death.
b: Brothers and helpers can fail in a crisis, but almsgiving "rescues." The Hebrew of manuscript B has "righteousness (tsedeq, margin tsedaqah) rescues," the words of Proverbs 10:2: "righteousness rescues from death." The angel in Tobit says "Alms rescue from death" (Tobit 12:9). Ben Sira has said that almsgiving atones for sins (3:30). How churches read such verses is set out on the card at Tobit 4 (top almsgiving).

a: but better than both is the fear of the Lord
t: The fear of the Lord at the top
p: The chain of "better than both" sayings ends where Ben Sira's whole book begins.
b: Ben Sira opened his book with the fear of the Lord as the beginning, fullness and crown of wisdom (1:11-20). Here it is better than wealth and strength, lacks nothing and needs no other help. The Hebrew of manuscript B has yir'at 'elohim, "the fear of God," and, in one line, the abbreviation for the divine name. Proverbs says the same: "the fear of the LORD is wisdom" (Job 28:28; compare Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 15:16).

a: like a paradise of blessing
p: The Greek paradeisos is the garden of Eden. The Hebrew says "like an Eden of blessing."
b: Paradeisos, a Persian word for a walled park, is what the Septuagint calls the garden of Eden (Genesis 2:8). The Hebrew of manuscript B has "The fear of God is like an Eden of blessing." Ben Sira uses the same picture for kindness at 40:17. The New Testament uses "paradise" for the place of the blessed with God (Luke 23:43; 2 Corinthians 12:4; Revelation 2:7).
orig: ὡς παράδεισος εὐλογίας (hōs paradeisos eulogias); Hebrew כעדן ברכה

a: do not live a beggar's life
p: Manuscript B writes in its margin near here a saying the Talmud quotes in Ben Sira's name: "even the nights."
b: Proverbs says, "For the afflicted every day is a hard one" (Proverbs 15:15). The Talmud (Sanhedrin 100b) quotes the Hebrew of that line, "All the days of the poor are evil," and adds: "Ben Sira says: Even the nights. His roof is at the lowest of roofs, and his vineyard on the height of the mountains." The rain runs off the other roofs onto his, and the soil of his vineyard washes down into theirs. The margin of manuscript B, beside 40:22-23, has the same saying, "Ben Sira says," with "even at night." The Greek does not have it. It shows that Ben Sira's sayings went about among Jews in forms longer than the grandson's book.

a: a life that cannot be counted as living
p: To live off another's table is not to live. The Hebrew uses the same words.
b: The Hebrew of manuscript B and the Masada scroll agree: "his life is not to be counted as life." A man who depends on another man's table eats food that "defiles his soul." This may mean the shame of it, or food that was not prepared by Jewish law, at a Gentile patron's table. The Hebrew of manuscript B goes on, "a delight to the soul is his food, / to a man who knows the secret of the inner parts," a hard line.
orig: οὐκ ἔστιν αὐτοῦ ὁ βίος ἐν λογισμῷ ζωῆς; Hebrew אין חייו למנות חיים

a: O death
p: Two short poems address death directly, first as bitter, then as welcome.
b: The Greek ō thanate, "O death," opens both 41:1 and 41:2. The Hebrew differs between the copies. At 41:1 manuscript B has "life" with hoy, "Ah!", in its margin, and the Masada scroll is damaged. At 41:2 Masada has "Ha, to death, how good..." and B has he'ach, "Aha!" Paul's cry, "Where, death, is your victory?" (1 Corinthians 15:55), addresses death too, but with the opposite hope.
orig: Ὦ θάνατε (Ō thanate); Masada at 41:2 הע למות

a: who prospers in everything
p: Job described the same two deaths: one in ease, one in bitterness.
b: Job says, "This man dies with his strength whole, / all of him at peace and untroubled," and "That man dies with bitterness in his soul" (Job 21:23-25). Ben Sira turns Job's complaint into a lesson. Death is bitter to the man at ease (41:1) and welcome to the old and worn-out (41:2), but it is the same sentence for both (41:3-4). Jesus' parable of the rich man who said "Soul, you have plenty" makes the first point sharply (Luke 12:19-20).

a: in Hades no one argues over the length of a life
t: Compared with the Bible: no questions in Hades
p: Ben Sira agrees with the Psalms and Ecclesiastes that Hades ends all striving. The New Testament goes further.
b: Agrees with the older books. In Sheol there is "no doing and no reckoning, no knowledge and no wisdom" (Ecclesiastes 9:10), and "among the dead no one calls you to mind" (Psalm 6:5). Ben Sira said the same at 17:27-28. Manuscript B (with the word "no" from its margin) and the Latin agree: "there are no arguments about life in Sheol." A long life or a short one makes no difference there. Differs from the New Testament, which speaks of "judgment" after death (Hebrews 9:27) and of the resurrection. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles also contain the Wisdom of Solomon (3:1-4) and 2 Maccabees 7, which go further. Protestant Bibles go from Ecclesiastes to the hope of Daniel 12:2.
orig: οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν ᾅδου ἐλεγμὸς ζωῆς; Hebrew אין תוכחות בשאול חיים
r: Ecclesiastes 9:10; Psalm 6:5; 17:27–28; Hebrews 9:27; Wisdom of Solomon 3:1–4; 2 Maccabees 7:9

a: ten years or a hundred or a thousand
p: No one in the Bible lived a thousand years. Methuselah came closest.
b: The oldest man in Genesis lived 969 years (Genesis 5:27), short of a thousand. A psalm says a thousand years in God's sight are "like yesterday" (Psalm 90:4). The Masada scroll's order is "ten, a hundred and a thousand years"; manuscript B has "a thousand years, a hundred and ten." The point is the same: once in Hades, the number no longer matters.

a: Hades
p: Hades is the Greek name for Sheol, the world of the dead.
b: The Greek hadēs renders the Hebrew she'ol, which Kahana's edition of manuscript B has here (the leaf is partly damaged). In the Hebrew Bible Sheol is the place where all the dead go, good and bad alike, a land of silence. The KJV of Sirach has "the grave." The New Testament uses Hades for the realm of the dead (Luke 16:23; Revelation 1:18).
orig: ᾅδης (hadēs); Hebrew שאול (she'ol)

a: who have abandoned the law of God Most High
p: In Ben Sira's lifetime some Jerusalem Jews were drawn to Greek ways. The woe may be aimed at them.
b: Ben Sira wrote around 180 BC, a few years before Jerusalem's leaders built a Greek gymnasium and "made a covenant with the nations" (1 Maccabees 1:11-15). Many scholars think his woes on those who "abandoned the law" are aimed at such Jews. The Masada scroll keeps the end of the line: "who forsake the law of the Most High," with the Hebrew torat 'elyon. Others read the woe as general, against the ungodly in every age, as in Psalm 1.

a: If you are born, you are born for a curse
p: The Hebrew has four lines here: on having children, stumbling and dying.
b: Manuscript B and the Masada scroll have a longer verse: "If you multiply, it is for disaster, / and if you bear children, it is for groaning. / If you stumble, it is for lasting joy, / and if you die, it is for a curse." The grandson's Greek has two lines. The thought follows the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28, which fall on the children and the work of those who turn from God.

a: Everything that comes from the earth goes back to the earth
p: The Greek repeats 40:11. The Hebrew says "from nothing to nothing" and "from chaos to chaos."
b: The first line is the same as 40:11 in the Greek. The Hebrew of manuscript B and the Masada scroll is different: "All that is from nothing returns to nothing, / so the godless man goes from chaos (tohu) to chaos." Tohu is the "shapeless" earth of Genesis 1:2 before God gave it form. The godless man comes from emptiness and goes back to it.
orig: Hebrew כל מאפס אל אפס ישוב / כן חנף מתהו אל תהו

a: but a good name remains for all time
p: A good name outlasts life. This is Ben Sira's hope after death.
b: "Better a good name than good oil" (Ecclesiastes 7:1), and "A name is worth choosing over great riches" (Proverbs 22:1). For Ben Sira a good name is more than reputation. It is the one part of a person that lasts (37:26; 39:9-11; 44:13-14). The Hebrew of manuscript B and the Masada scroll has "The good of life is a number of days, / but the good of a name, days without number," which echoes 37:25.

a: Wisdom kept hidden and treasure out of sight
p: The Greek of 41:14b-15 repeats 20:30-31 word for word.
b: Ben Sira, or his grandson, uses the same pair of sayings twice: hidden wisdom is like buried treasure, and it is better to hide your folly than your wisdom (20:30-31). Jesus' parable of the buried talent makes a similar point (Matthew 25:25-27). In the Hebrew of manuscript B and the Masada scroll these lines come after the heading of 41:14a, "Listen, children, to instruction about shame." The Greek's "in peace" may come from reading a different Hebrew word.

a: it is not good to keep every kind of shame
p: 41:16-42:8 lists what to be ashamed of, and what not to be ashamed of.
b: Ben Sira teaches that shame is a good guard when it keeps a person from sin (41:17-42:1), and a bad master when it keeps him from doing right (42:1-8). He said the same earlier: "There is one kind of shame that leads a person into sin, / and another kind of shame that is honor and grace" (4:21). The Hebrew of manuscript B has "not every shame is fitting to keep." The section was clearly important to later Jewish scribes, since manuscript C copies a line of it as well.

a: of leaning your elbow on the bread at a meal
p: Among the things to be ashamed of: elbows on the bread and rudeness at table.
b: The Hebrew of manuscript B and the Masada scroll has "of stretching out the elbow over the bread." At meals, people reclined or sat around a shared table and took bread from a common plate. To spread one's arm across the food was greedy and rude. Ben Sira has a whole section of advice on banquets (34:12-35:13).

a: of meddling with a man's slave girl
p: Ben Sira warns against sex with a slave woman, which the law and the custom of the time did not always forbid.
b: In the ancient world a master could use his slave women, and the Bible records cases (Genesis 16:2; Genesis 30:3). The law gave some protection to slave women (Exodus 21:7-11; Leviticus 19:20). Ben Sira treats such meddling as shameful, with an added command, "do not go near her bed." The Masada scroll has the same command, "of standing over her bed."

a: But do not be ashamed of these things
t: Do not be ashamed of these
p: The list turns: here are things a person should do without shame, even if others mock.
b: The second list (42:1-8) covers the law, honest courts, accounts and business, discipline at home and correcting fools. In each, social pressure might make a person shy: favoritism to the powerful, embarrassment about money, softness with children. The Hebrew of manuscript B and the Masada scroll begins, "But of these do not be ashamed, / and do not show partiality and sin." Partiality, literally "lifting the face," is forbidden to judges by the law (Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 1:17).

a: a judgment that gives the ungodly his due
p: The Greek says literally "a judgment to justify the ungodly," which seems to clash with Proverbs 17:15.
b: Proverbs condemns "Declaring the wicked innocent" (Proverbs 17:15). How can Ben Sira tell his pupil not to be ashamed "to justify the ungodly"? Readers take it three ways. (1) Do not be ashamed to judge fairly, even if that means acquitting a man of bad character who is innocent of this charge. (2) Do not be ashamed to give the ungodly the sentence that is just, "his due," which is how the Plain takes it. (3) The Greek is a stiff rendering of a Hebrew idiom. The Masada scroll reads "and of justice, to declare the wicked in the right" (or "to do justice to the wicked"). Paul's "God who justifies the ungodly" (Romans 4:5) is a different matter and a different word-setting.
orig: περὶ κρίματος δικαιῶσαι τὸν ἀσεβῆ; Masada ועל משפט להצדיק רשע

a: of beating a bad slave until his side bleeds
t: Compared with the Bible: beating slaves
p: Ben Sira accepts harsh punishment of slaves. The law limited it, and the New Testament reshapes the master's place.
b: Agrees with the setting of the Hebrew Bible, which allowed slavery and beating (Exodus 21:20-21). The law limited it: a master whose slave died under the rod was punished, and a slave who lost an eye went free (Exodus 21:20, 26). Ben Sira himself also says, "If you have a slave, let him be like yourself" (30:39). The New Testament reshapes it: masters are to stop threatening, since slave and master have one Lord (Ephesians 6:9), and in Christ there is "no slave and no free person" (Galatians 3:28). Every church today rejects slavery. Readers of every tradition read this line as a witness to its time.
r: Exodus 21:20–21; Exodus 21:26–27; 30:33–40; Ephesians 6:9; Galatians 3:28; Philemon 16; Proverbs 29:19

a: Put a seal on things where the wife is bad
p: Storerooms were closed with a clay seal. A broken seal showed someone had been inside.
b: A household's goods were kept in jars and storerooms closed with clay pressed with a seal, as the lion pit was sealed in Daniel 6:17 and the tomb in Matthew 27:66. A broken seal showed tampering. Ben Sira's advice is to protect property where a wife or many servants cannot be trusted. The Hebrew of manuscript B reads "a seal is wise" over "a foolish wife" (in the margin), and the Masada scroll has "a seal" with "many hands."

a: that she may be hated
p: In biblical law, a husband who "hates" his wife is one who sends her away.
b: The Greek misēthē, "be hated," carries the meaning of the Hebrew sane' in marriage law: "the second man hates her, writes her a certificate of divorce" (Deuteronomy 24:3). The father fears that his married daughter will be divorced and come home in disgrace. Each line of 42:9-10 names a stage of her life: girlhood, betrothal, marriage, childbearing. The Talmud quotes a form of these lines in Ben Sira's name and calls the daughter "false treasure" to her father (Sanhedrin 100b).
orig: μή ποτε μισηθῇ (mē pote misēthē)

a: A daughter keeps her father awake in secret
p: Rav Yosef said it was forbidden to read Ben Sira; Abaye asked why, and quoted this passage among others.
b: The Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 100b) records that Rav Yosef said it is forbidden to read the book of Ben Sira. Abaye asked what the problem could be, and among other lines cited: "A daughter is for her father false treasure; due to fear for her he will not sleep at night," with the stages of her life (Sefaria's translation). He answered that the rabbis said similar things. Rav Yosef then said that the good things in Ben Sira may still be taught in public, and quoted several. So Ben Sira was both read and doubted by the rabbis. The Talmud's form of the daughter passage differs from both the Greek and the Hebrew manuscripts.

a: Do not look at anyone for their beauty
p: In the Greek the reader is told not to look; in the Hebrew the daughter is not to show her beauty to any male.
b: The Greek speaks to the reader: do not stare at people for their looks, and do not sit among women. The Hebrew of manuscript B is still about the daughter: "Let her not show her beauty to any male, / and let her not sit and talk in the house of women." The Masada scroll's first line reads "Let her not look at the form of any male." The grandson either read the Hebrew differently or broadened it into advice for the young men he was writing for.
orig: παντὶ ἀνθρώπῳ μὴ ἔμβλεπε ἐν κάλλει; Hebrew לכל זכר אל תתן תאר

a: For the moth comes out of clothes
p: A moth hatches in the very cloth it eats. So a woman's wickedness grows from women's company.
b: The moth's larva grows inside clothing and eats it from within. Jesus uses the moth as a picture of how earthly treasure is destroyed (Matthew 6:19). Ben Sira's point, in its setting, is that a daughter learns bad ways from other women (42:12). The Masada scroll writes sas, the rare word for a moth larva (Isaiah 51:8), where manuscript B has 'ash, the common word.

a: Better a man's wickedness than a woman who does good
t: Compared with the Bible: a man's wickedness and a woman's goodness
p: One of the harshest lines about women in Ben Sira. It conflicts with the Bible's praise of good women.
b: The Greek says it is better to have a man's wickedness than a good woman. The Hebrew of manuscript B and the Masada scroll say the same in their first line: "Better the evil of a man than the good of a woman." Their second lines differ from each other and are hard to read. Read in its setting (42:9-13), the saying may mean that a young man is safer with a harsh man than with a kind woman. Read alone, it conflicts with the Bible's praise of women who do good, from the woman of strength (Proverbs 31:10, 30-31) to Ruth, Abigail and the women of the Gospels, and with Genesis 1:27 and Galatians 3:28. Readers in every tradition have had to weigh this line against those passages.
r: 42:9–13; Proverbs 31:10; Proverbs 31:30–31; Genesis 1:27; Galatians 3:28; Ruth 3:11; Luke 8:1–3

a: I will remember the Lord's works now
p: 42:15-43:33 is a hymn on God's works in the sky, the weather and the sea. The Masada scroll preserves most of it.
b: The hymn opens the last section of the book: first God's works in nature (42:15-43:33), then his works in history, the Praise of the Fathers (44-50). It moves from God's knowledge (42:18-21) to the sun, moon, stars and rainbow (43:1-12), the snow, storm and frost (43:13-22) and the sea (43:23-26), and ends in praise beyond words (43:27-33). The Masada scroll, copied before AD 73, has much of it in columns V and VI. Manuscript B of the Genizah has all of it. The Catholic weekday lectionary reads 42:15-25 on Thursday of the Eighth Week in Ordinary Time (lectionary 350).

a: His works exist by the Lord's words
t: Created by the word, and Masada's "Adonai"
p: God made his works by speaking. The Masada copy writes the divine name as "Adonai."
b: "The heavens were made by the LORD's word" (Psalm 33:6), and in Genesis 1 God speaks and things come to be. The Masada scroll reads "By the word of Adonai are his works." Throughout the hymn it writes 'adonai, "Lord" (42:15, 16, 17; 43:5, 10), where manuscript B has 'elohim, "God," or the abbreviation of the divine name. Manuscript B's third line reads "by the word of God, his will." The Greek "the Lord" fits either form. On the names, see the note on 37:15.
orig: ἐν λόγοις Κυρίου τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ; Masada באמר אדני מעשיו

a: his work is filled with his glory
p: The Masada scroll reads "the glory of the Lord fills his works," like the seraphim's song.
b: The sun shines on everything, and God's work is full of his glory. The Masada scroll has "the glory of Adonai fills his works." The seraphim cry, "Everything that fills the earth is his glory" (Isaiah 6:3), and the psalm says "The heavens keep recounting God's glory" (Psalm 19:1). The Greek sun-image prepares for the sun's own stanza in 43:2-5.

a: Not even to his holy ones has the Lord granted
t: Holy ones and the Lord of armies
p: The "holy ones" are angels. The Masada Hebrew plays on God's title "the Lord of Armies."
b: "Holy ones" means the angels, as in Job 5:1 and Psalm 89:7. Even they cannot recount all God's wonders. The Greek "the Lord Almighty" (pantokratōr) is the Septuagint's usual rendering of "the LORD of Armies." The Masada scroll has "Adonai has strengthened his armies (tseva'av) / to stand firm before his glory," so the Hebrew line is built on that very title. Manuscript B has the same with 'elohim.
orig: τοῖς ἁγίοις (tois hagiois); Κύριος ὁ παντοκράτωρ; Masada אמץ אדני צבאיו

a: He has searched out the deep and the heart
p: God knows the depths of the sea and of the human heart alike.
b: The deep (abyssos, Hebrew tehom) is the ocean under the world (Genesis 1:2). The heart is the hidden self. God searches both (Psalm 139:1-12; Jeremiah 17:10). The Masada scroll and manuscript B read "The deep and the heart he searches out, / and all their secrets he understands." Proverbs says the human breath is the LORD's lamp searching the inner rooms (Proverbs 20:27).

a: for he is from before the ages and for all ages
p: The Masada Hebrew says "He is One from eternity," an echo of the Shema.
b: The Greek is hard (literally "and as he is before the age and to the age"). Manuscript B reads "He is One from eternity," with 'echad, "one," the word of the Shema: "The LORD is our God. The LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4). God needs no counselor (Isaiah 40:13-14), and nothing can be added to or taken away from what he does (Ecclesiastes 3:14).
orig: Masada אחד הוא מעולם

a: Everything is double, one thing facing another
p: Ben Sira sees creation in pairs: good and evil, life and death, each balancing the other.
b: He said it before: "look at all the works of the Most High, two by two, one opposite the other" (36:15). The pairs explain how harmful things fit a good creation (39:16-35): each thing "makes the good of the other stronger" (42:25). Some scholars compare Greek ideas of balanced opposites. Others see it as a reading of Genesis 1, where God makes day and night, sea and land. The Hebrew of manuscript B says "all of them differ one from another," and the Masada scroll has "one facing the other."

a: the clear, firm dome
p: The Greek stereōma, like the Hebrew raqia', is the solid-looking vault of the sky.
b: Genesis calls the sky a "dome" (raqia', Greek stereōma, "firm thing"), set in the middle of the waters (Genesis 1:6). The Masada scroll has "the form of the height and the dome (raqia') in its purity." Ancient people saw the sky as a solid vault. Readers differ on whether the Bible teaches that picture or uses the language of how things look. The Plain uses "dome" as the site does in Genesis.
orig: στερέωμα (stereōma); Masada רקיע

a: an amazing instrument, the work of the Most High
p: The sun is a marvelous instrument, as in Psalm 19, but never a god.
b: Many of Israel's neighbors worshiped the sun. The Bible praises it as God's work and servant (Genesis 1:16; Psalm 19:4-6; Psalm 104:19). The Masada scroll agrees with the Greek: "an awesome instrument, the work of the Most High." Ben Sira's sun hymn (43:2-5) moves from its rising to its heat at noon and ends: "Great is the Lord who made it." The Wisdom of Solomon makes the same argument against nature-worship (Wisdom of Solomon 13:2-5).
r: Genesis 1:16; Psalm 19:4–6; Psalm 104:19; Deuteronomy 4:19; Wisdom of Solomon 13:2–5

a: The stoker of a furnace works amid the heat
p: Ben Sira compares the sun to a smith's furnace, which he described in 38:28.
b: The image picks up the smith of 38:28, who "battles the furnace's heat." The sun is three times hotter and sets the hills ablaze. The Hebrew of manuscript B begins "a blown furnace," a furnace fanned with bellows. The line "its flashing beams dim the sight" is a warning that every child knows: do not look into the sun.

a: The moon, too, keeps to its time in everything
p: Ben Sira says the moon fixes the seasons and feasts. Some Jews of his day held to a calendar based on the sun.
b: The months of Israel began with the new moon, and the feasts were set by it (Psalm 104:19; Leviticus 23). Ben Sira says so plainly: "The moon gives the sign for the feasts" (43:7). The book of 1 Enoch (chapters 72-82) and Jubilees teach a year of 364 days counted by the sun, and the calendar page describes that dispute. Ben Sira, a Jerusalem scribe who loved the Temple (50:1-21), stands with the moon.
r: Psalm 104:19; Genesis 1:14; Leviticus 23:2–4; Numbers 28:11; 1 Enoch 72:1; Jubilees 6:36

a: The month is named after the moon
p: In both Greek and Hebrew, the word for "month" is tied to the moon.
b: In Greek mēn, "month," is close to mēnē, "moon." In Hebrew chodesh means both "new moon" and "month," from the root "to be new." The Masada scroll reads "The new moon (chodesh), as its name says, renews itself (mitchaddesh)." The Greek turns that wordplay into its own: the month is named after the moon. The second half of the verse, "a signal for the camps on high," is in the variant.
orig: μὴν κατὰ τὸ ὄνομα αὐτῆς; Masada חדש כשמו הוא מת[חדש]

a: they do not tire on their watch
p: The stars are soldiers or watchmen at their posts, never sleeping.
b: Baruch says, "The stars shone out, each at its post, and were full of joy. / He called them, and they answered, 'Here we are!'" (Baruch 3:34-35). Isaiah says God "marches their army out by count / and calls each one by name" (Isaiah 40:26). The Masada scroll has "By the word of Adonai the law stands, / and they do not sink down at their watches."

a: Look at the rainbow and bless the one who made it
p: The rainbow is the sign of God's covenant with Noah. Ezekiel and Revelation see it around God's throne.
b: After the flood God said, "my bow I have put in the clouds, and it will be the sign of a covenant between me and the earth" (Genesis 9:13). The Greek and Hebrew both call it simply "the bow" (toxon, qeshet), the same word as a hunter's bow. Ezekiel saw God's glory "Like the look of the bow that is in the clouds on a day of rain" (Ezekiel 1:28), and John saw "around the throne" a rainbow (Revelation 4:3). Ben Sira tells the reader to bless God at the sight.

a: the Most High's hands drew it taut
p: The verb tanyō is used for drawing a bowstring. The rainbow is God's bow, bent and hung up.
b: The Greek etanysan, "stretched," is the verb for stringing and drawing a bow. The prophets picture God with a bow (Habakkuk 3:9). In Genesis 9 the bow in the clouds is a sign of peace. The Masada scroll says "the hand of God stretched it out in might."
orig: ἐτάνυσαν (etanysan)

a: By his command he makes the snow settle
p: The Greek begins with snow. The Hebrew begins with lightning (B) or hail (Masada).
b: Swete's Vaticanus reads katepausen, "made rest, settled," the snow. A corrector of Vaticanus and Alexandrinus and Ephraemi have katespeusen, "hurried." The Hebrew of manuscript B reads "His might marks out the lightning," and the Masada scroll "His rebuke marks out the hail" (barad). The Hebrew words for lightning (baraq) and hail (barad) differ by one similar letter. The Greek "snow" fits the snow stanza that follows (43:17-18).
orig: κατέπαυσεν χιόνα (katepausen chiona); Hebrew B ברק, Masada ברד

a: So his treasure-houses swing open
p: Snow, hail and wind are kept in God's storehouses, as in Job 38.
b: God asks Job, "Have you walked into the places where snow is stored? / Have you looked where hail is kept" (Job 38:22). Jeremiah says he "leads the wind out of its storerooms" (Jeremiah 10:13). Ben Sira pictures the doors flung open and the clouds flying out like birds. The Masada scroll reads "the clouds fly like a bird of prey."

a: The mountains are shaken at the sight of him
t: The order of the storm lines
p: The Greek, manuscript B and the Masada scroll put the lines of 43:16-17 in different orders.
b: In the Greek, the mountains shake and the south wind blows (43:16), then the thunder rebukes the earth (43:17). The Masada scroll has the thunder first: "The sound of his thunder makes his earth writhe, / and by his strength he shakes the mountains. / His word makes the south wind (teman) blow sharp, / the whirlwind of the storm and tempest." Manuscript B has a third order. The Plain keeps the Greek order, which is the one the churches received.

a: it falls the way locusts settle
p: Snow drifts down like birds landing and covers the ground like a swarm of locusts.
b: The psalm says God "lays down snow like wool" (Psalm 147:16). Ben Sira has two pictures: birds swooping down, and locusts settling. A locust swarm, which could cover the land until "no one could see the ground" (Exodus 10:5), is a strong image of a heavy snowfall. The Masada scroll agrees, "and like locusts it settles as it comes down." Snow falls on the hills around Jerusalem in some winters.

a: it becomes sharp points like thorns
p: The Masada scroll says the frost sprouts points "like a thornbush" (seneh), the word for the burning bush.
b: The Greek has "points of thorns." Manuscript B reads "and it blossoms like sapphire (or 'like a flower') blossoms," while the Masada scroll reads "and it sprouts points like a thornbush," with seneh, the rare word for the bush that burned before Moses (Exodus 3:2). Here the older Masada text agrees with the Greek against manuscript B, and shows what the grandson read. Frost forms needle-like crystals on plants on cold mornings.
orig: σκολόπων ἄκρα (skolopōn akra); Masada כסנה צצים

a: the water dresses in it like a breastplate
p: Ice covers a pond as a breastplate covers a soldier.
b: The breastplate (thōrax) was a soldier's armor for the chest. A pool frozen over looks as if it had put on armor. The Hebrew of manuscript B has "and like a coat of mail it clothes the pool." Job asks, "Whose womb does the ice come out of?" (Job 38:29), and the psalm says, "He flings his ice like bits of bread; / who can stand up to his cold?" (Psalm 147:17).

a: dew that comes after the heat brings refreshment
p: In a dry land, dew and mist after a hot day were a healing gift.
b: In the dry summer of the land of Israel, when no rain falls for months, night dew waters the plants. Hosea promises, "I will be like the dew for Israel" (Hosea 14:5). Manuscript B reads "The healing of all is the drip of a cloud, / dew that breaks out to refresh after the heat." After the scorching wind of 43:21, the mist comes as healing (iasis), the same word as the doctor's healing in 38:2.

a: His thinking quieted the deep
p: God's thought stilled the sea. Jesus does the same with a word.
b: Psalm 107 tells of sailors in a storm: God "spoke and stood up a storm wind" (Psalm 107:25), and then hushed it. Job says, "By his power he quelled the sea" (Job 26:12). In the Gospels Jesus rebukes the wind and the sea, and "there was a great calm" (Mark 4:39). In the Gospel, Jesus does with a word what Ben Sira says God does by his thought.

a: Sailors on the sea tell how dangerous it is
p: Israel was not a seafaring nation. Its writers spoke of the sea with awe.
b: Few Israelites were sailors. Jonah's voyage and Paul's shipwreck (Acts 27) are the Bible's great sea stories. Psalm 107:23-24 says those who "took ships down to the sea" "saw what the LORD does." Ben Sira knows the sea from sailors' tales, "what reaches our ears." The Masada scroll keeps the end of the line: "at what our ears hear, we are astonished."

a: by his word all things are put together
t: All things put together by his word
p: The Greek synkeitai, "lie together, are put together," anticipates the New Testament's language for Christ.
b: Ben Sira says that by God's word everything is held in its place. Christian writers use similar language of Christ: "all things hold together in him" (Colossians 1:17), and "he carries all things along by his word of power" (Hebrews 1:3). The words differ (Colossians has synestēken), but the thought is close. Compare John 1:3: "Through him everything came to exist."
orig: ἐν λόγῳ αὐτοῦ σύνκειται πάντα (en logō autou synkeitai panta)
r: Colossians 1:17; Hebrews 1:3; John 1:3; Psalm 33:6; Wisdom of Solomon 1:7

a: "He is the all."
p: The most famous line of the hymn. It means God is the sum and source of all, not that all is God.
b: The Greek to pan estin autos sounds like the Stoic teaching that God is the world. Ben Sira does not mean that, since the whole hymn distinguishes the Maker from his works: "He is the Great One, beyond all his works" (43:28). The Hebrew of manuscript B reads "and the end of the matter: He is the all" (veqets davar hu' hakol), close to the last words of Ecclesiastes, "The last word, now that everything has been heard" (Ecclesiastes 12:13), which in Hebrew begin sof davar hakol. Paul's "so that God may be all in all" (1 Corinthians 15:28) and "everything is from him, and through him, and for him" (Romans 11:36) are the New Testament's way of saying it.
orig: Τὸ πᾶν ἐστιν αὐτός (To pan estin autos); Hebrew וקץ דבר הוא הכל

a: Who has seen him, to describe him?
p: No one has seen God to describe him. John's Gospel says the Son has made him known.
b: Ben Sira ends where the Bible's wisdom always ends: God is beyond human sight and speech (Job 26:14; Psalm 145:3). John's Gospel says the same, then adds: "Nobody has ever seen God. It is the only one, God, the one in the Father's embrace, who has made him known" (John 1:18).

a: he gave wisdom to the godly
p: The last line points ahead: the godly to whom God gave wisdom are the fathers praised in chapters 44-50.
b: The hymn ends with wisdom given "to the godly." At once Ben Sira begins, "Let us now praise famous men" (44:1). Kahana's edition of manuscript B has "and to those who fear him he gave wisdom," followed by the heading "Praise of the Fathers of Old." The Latin Vulgate numbers this chapter differently, so its last verse here is 43:37.
